name: Delhi
info: Delhi is a city on the Yamuna river in northern India, with a recorded history from the Tomara rulers of the 11th century, the capital of the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal Empire, and now of the Republic of India.

facts.founded: Anang Pal of the Tomara dynasty built Lal Kot in 1052 CE; the Tomaras are placed earlier too, and tradition links the site with Indraprastha, the city of the Mahabharata.
facts.where: On the Yamuna river, chiefly on its right bank, between the Yamuna floodplains and the Delhi Ridge, in northern India.
facts.known: Capital of the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal Empire; the Qutub Minar, the Red Fort and Humayun’s Tomb; Sufism and qawwali; Urdu poetry; the sacks of 1398 and 1739; the rebellion of 1857; New Delhi, the capital of India
facts.today: Delhi is the National Capital Territory of India and contains New Delhi, the capital of the country.

t: Delhi was built, destroyed and rebuilt several times, and tradition counts seven cities on its site, from the Tomara fort of 1052 to Shah Jahan’s Shahjahanabad.
It was the capital of the Delhi Sultanate from 1206 and of the Mughal Empire from 1638, and it was sacked by Timur in 1398 and by Nader Shah in 1739.
Britain moved its Indian capital to Delhi in 1911, and after Partition in 1947 the city changed from a Mughal city to a Punjabi one.
dyk: Excavations at Purana Qila, which tradition identifies with the Indraprastha of the Mahabharata, have found painted grey pottery of the 11th century BCE but no sign of a built environment or fortifications.
ev: Anang Pal of the Tomara dynasty builds Lal Kot
Qutb-ud-din Aibak founds the Delhi Sultanate with Delhi as its capital
Shah Jahan makes Shahjahanabad the Mughal capital
Nader Shah sacks and loots the city
Rebels hold Delhi until British troops retake it in September
The capital of British India is announced to be moving to Delhi
New Delhi becomes the capital of independent India

sections.origins:
Delhi lies on the Yamuna river, chiefly on its right bank, between the Yamuna floodplains and the Delhi Ridge, which runs out of the Aravalli Range. Carbon dating places an Ochre Coloured Pottery culture in the area of the Red Fort from about 2000 BCE, and people of the Painted Grey Ware culture, which corresponds to the Vedic period, lived in the region around 1200 BCE.

A long tradition identifies the place with Indraprastha, the city of the Sanskrit epic Mahabharata, which was composed between about 400 BCE and 300 CE but describes an earlier time. The topography of Purana Qila matches the epic’s description, and a village called Indarpat survived inside the fort into the early 20th century. Excavations, however, have found painted grey pottery of the 11th century BCE and no sign of a built environment or fortifications. Buddhist literature of the Mauryan period called the city Indapatta, and an inscription of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka was found near Srinivaspuri in 1966.

There are several legends of the name Delhi, among them a king called Dhillu or Dilu who built a city here in 50 BCE, and the Prakrit word dhili (loose). The Tomara Rajput king Anang Pal built Lal Kot and several temples in 1052 CE. The Chauhans of Ajmer later took Lal Kot and renamed it Qila Rai Pithora.
sections.growth:
Delhi grew as a series of cities, traditionally counted as seven. After 1206 Qutb-ud-din Aibak began the Qutub Minar and the Quwwat-al-Islam mosque, the earliest surviving mosque in India. The tower, 72.5 m high, was finished in the 13th century under Iltutmish. The sultans who followed built a sequence of forts and townships, and the sultanate reached its greatest extent under Muhammad bin Tughluq (1325 to 1351). In the 14th century Firuz Shah Tughluq brought two sandstone pillars inscribed with the edicts of Ashoka to the city.

In the 16th century Sher Shah Suri built the sixth city and the fort known as Purana Qila, on a site settled since ancient times. The Mughals ruled at first from Agra, Sikri and Lahore, and built Humayun’s Tomb in Delhi. The largest change came when Shah Jahan built Shahjahanabad, the seventh city, now the Old City, with the Red Fort and the Jama Masjid. The mosque was built in 1656 and is described as the largest in India. Shah Jahan made the city his capital from 1638. Chandni Chowk, a 17th-century market, is known for jewellery and zari saris, and the city’s crafts include zardozi, embroidery in gold thread, and meenakari, enamelling.

The 18th century added the Jantar Mantar, an astronomical observatory. After 1911 the British built another city to the south, New Delhi, designed by Edwin Lutyens.
sections.rulers:
The recorded history of Delhi begins with the Tomara dynasty, placed by one reckoning from 736 to 1193. The Chauhans held the city until Prithviraj III was defeated by Muhammad Ghori in 1192 at the Second Battle of Tarain. In 1206 Qutb-ud-din Aibak, a former slave who had risen to be a general and a governor, founded the Delhi Sultanate and its Mamluk dynasty. Five dynasties held Delhi as capital: the Mamluks, the Khaljis (from 1290), the Tughluqs, the Sayyids (1414 to 1451) and the Lodis (1451 to 1526). Razia, the daughter of Iltutmish, became Sultana of Delhi on his death.

Babur defeated the last Lodi sultan at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526, and the early Mughals ruled from Agra and Lahore. Sher Shah Suri drove Humayun out, and his son Islam Shah ruled from Delhi. In 1556 Hemu defeated Akbar’s army at Delhi and took the throne, but lost the Second Battle of Panipat. Akbar ruled from Agra. Shah Jahan returned the capital to Delhi, and Aurangzeb crowned himself there in 1658.

After 1707 the empire weakened. A treaty of 1752 made the Marathas protectors of the Mughal throne, and the city was taken in turn by Jats (1753), Ahmad Shah Durrani (1757 and 1761), the Marathas and, briefly, the Sikhs in 1783. The British East India Company defeated the Marathas in 1803, and the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II remained a figurehead. Direct British rule followed the rebellion of 1857.
sections.life:
Delhi was a major centre of Sufism under the sultans, and the names of Nizamuddin Auliya and Amir Khusrau are prominently associated with its Sufi tradition and with qawwali music. The Khariboli dialect of Delhi was part of a linguistic development that gave rise to Urdu and later to Modern Standard Hindi. Mir Taqi Mir and Mirza Ghalib are counted among the major Urdu poets of the city, and Dard, Dagh and Zauq lived there and sought the emperor’s patronage.

Its monuments record the faiths of its rulers. Qutb-ud-din Aibak is said to have destroyed twenty-seven Jain temples in the Qutb complex and to have used their carved pillars and building material for the mosque, and many of the pillars can still be seen. Some palatial residences, the havelis, stand in the Old City.

The city changed in population as well as in buildings. During the partition of India in 1947 about 500,000 Hindu and Sikh refugees, mainly from West Punjab, came to Delhi, and about 300,000 of the city’s Muslim residents went to Pakistan. It has been described as a change from a Mughal city to a Punjabi one, with the loss of two-thirds of its Muslim residents, in part through pressure from the arriving refugees. Hindi is now the most spoken language, and Urdu and Punjabi are additional official languages.
sections.crises:
Delhi was sacked more than once. In 1398 Timur invaded India on the pretext that the sultans of Delhi were too tolerant of their Hindu subjects. He defeated the army of Nasiruddin Mahmud of the Tughluq dynasty and entered Delhi on 18 December 1398. The city was sacked and left in ruins, and 100,000 or more captives are said to have been killed. In 1737 Maratha forces under Baji Rao I sacked Delhi after defeating the Mughals.

In 1739 the Persian army of Nader Shah beat the Mughals at Karnal in less than three hours and then took Delhi. He sacked and looted the city, and a massacre of two days is said to have killed over 30,000 civilians. He carried off the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor, and left only after the emperor Muhammad Shah I begged for mercy and handed over the keys of the city and the royal treasury. The Jats sacked the city from 9 May to 4 June 1753, and Ahmad Shah Durrani’s forces took it in 1757.

In the rebellion of 1857 mutineers reached Delhi on 11 May and declared Bahadur Shah Zafar emperor. British forces laid siege to the city on 8 June and took it on 21 September, and it was significantly damaged. The last Mughal emperor was captured and exiled to Rangoon. The anti-Sikh pogroms of 1984, set off by the assassination of Indira Gandhi, killed around 2,800 people in Delhi according to government figures, and independent estimates are higher.
sections.legacy:
Three World Heritage Sites in the city, the Qutub Minar, Humayun’s Tomb and the Red Fort, all belong to the sultanate and Mughal periods. The Archaeological Survey of India recognises 1,200 heritage buildings and 175 monuments in Delhi as national heritage sites. A saying of the Northern Indo-Aryan languages, that Delhi is still far away, is used of a task far from finished.

The move of the capital of British India from Calcutta to Delhi was announced by George V at the Delhi Durbar of 1911 and formally made on 12 December 1911. The new city received the name New Delhi in 1927 and was inaugurated on 13 February 1931. The project met opposition from the European business community of Calcutta, from Lord Curzon and from Mahatma Gandhi. The part built in the British period is informally known as Lutyens’ Delhi. New Delhi became the capital of independent India in 1947.

Delhi became a union territory in 1956, and the Constitution (Sixty-ninth Amendment) Act of 1991 named it the National Capital Territory. It contains New Delhi, the capital of India. The territory has some 17 million people, and over 11 million of them live in the city proper.

summary: Delhi, on the Yamuna river, was rebuilt in several successive cities, from a Tomara fort of 1052 to Shah Jahan’s Shahjahanabad and Lutyens’ New Delhi. It was the capital of the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal Empire, was sacked by Timur and Nader Shah, and is the capital of India.
notes: START: delhi.txt and History of Delhi both say Anang Pal Tomar built Lal Kot/founded Delhi in 1052; History of Delhi also says the Tomar dynasty was established in the early 8th century and ruled 736 to 1193, and that recorded history begins with the 8th century. I used 1052 as the start and did not set circa.
The Chauhan conquest of Lal Kot: History of Delhi says 1180; Delhi says the mid-12th century under Vigraharaja IV. I wrote only "later", without a year.
Shah Jahan's capital: History of Delhi gives both 1648 and 1638; Delhi says 1638. I used 1638.

Ashoka's reign is given as 273-236 BCE and 273-235 BCE: left out. Timur entered Delhi 18 December 1398 (both); History of Delhi adds that he defeated Nasiruddin Mahmud on 15 December. Captives killed: "over 100,000 war prisoners" (History) and "100,000 captive civilians" (Delhi); I wrote 100,000 or more captives.
Nader Shah: the "over 30,000 civilians" in two days comes only from History of Delhi, so I attributed it ("one article says"). Delhi gives no figure. Both articles hedge nothing about it.
The Quwwat-al-Islam and the 27 Jain temples: History of Delhi says "He was said to have destroyed"; I kept that hedge.
Delhi's legal status: Delhi lead says NCT "in 1995"; both articles also say the Sixty-ninth Amendment Act of 1991. I used 1991 as the Act and did not give 1995.
The 2020 riots, the 2001 and 2005/2008 attacks, the 2026 protests, 1973-74 riots were left out as present-day or minor; 1984 pogrom included with the article's figure and hedge.

The Delhi Durbar: History of Delhi says King George V announced the move at the 1911 Durbar; Delhi says "formally transferred on 12 December 1911". New Delhi inaugurated 1931 (both), named 1927 (Delhi), "officially declared seat of government after independence in 1947".
Population: no pre-modern figures in either article. 2011 census figures only.

Not found: the date of the Qutub Minar's start beyond "after 1206"; Mughal era population; Tughlaqabad, Siri and Firuzabad by name (the articles only say "forts and townships"); Jama Masjid builder named (not stated; the article gives only 1656 and India's largest mosque).
